title-group.article-title: Comments on: Low adherence to aspirin and calcium carbonate for preeclampsia prevention in pregnant women with chronic hypertension in a Brazilian hospital

body.p: We read with interest the article "Low adherence to aspirin and calcium carbonate for preeclampsia prevention in pregnant women with chronic hypertension in a Brazilian hospital," published by Jardine et al.(1) The authors concluded that there was low adherence to aspirin and calcium carbonate prophylaxis among pregnant women with chronic hypertension, with no significant difference in preeclampsia (PE) rates between adherent and non-adherent groups. Furthermore, they wonder about the effectiveness of aspirin prophylaxis in women with chronic hypertension. In this letter, we raise concerns about the misinterpretation of the results obtained and its possible downstream consequences.

The study is valuable in highlighting the importance of assessing adherence to prophylactic medications through a qualitative instrument. However, assessment of prophylaxis efficacy loses its value when adherence is lacking. The conclusions should not be misinterpreted solely because no difference in outcomes was observed between the groups with and without adherence, especially given that (i) aspirin may significantly delay gestational age at birth without modifying the crude rate of PE, and (ii) as recent evidence suggests that calcium does not reduce the risk of PE, adherence to calcium prophylaxis becomes irrelevant.

After the ASPRE trial,(2) it has been established that aspirin prophylaxis is the gold-standard approach for preventing preterm PE among high-risk women. The risk of preterm PE can be estimated at 11–14 weeks of gestation by using an algorithm freely provided by the Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF)(3) that combines data from maternal characteristics and medical history with biophysical and biochemical markers.

In 2017, a secondary analysis(4) of the Aspirin for Evidence-based Preeclampsia Prevention (ASPRE) trial(2) suggested that the beneficial effect of aspirin in the prevention of preterm PE may not apply to pregnancies with chronic hypertension. Without an obvious mechanism to explain this lack of effect in women with chronic hypertension, Bujold et al.(5) performed a post hoc secondary analysis of ASPRE trial results in 2025 and found that women with chronic hypertension benefit from aspirin during pregnancy by reducing the earliest cases of PE, and shifting the distribution of gestational age at birth due to PE. Thus, caution is warranted when minimizing the effect of low-dose aspirin in pregnant women with chronic hypertension, as there is demonstrated benefit for those identified through the FMF algorithm.

Compliance with prophylactic measures is paramount for the success of the intervention, as previously demonstrated in the ASPRE trial(2,6) and emphasized by the authors.(1) The observed low adherence, approximately 40%, to aspirin or calcium reflects a natural resistance among pregnant women(7) in contemporary real-world settings to generic interventions, such as the use of aspirin based on clinical criteria proposed by the World Health Organization (WHO)(8) through checklists, and the universal calcium supplementation recommended by the Brazilian Ministry of Health.(9) Low adherence and the consequent lack of effectiveness in reducing PE and its associated outcomes are to be expected when prescribing is uniform rather than individualized, as also observed in a Canadian study(10) that assessed adherence to aspirin when recommended for pregnant women with clinical risk factors and showed that only 27% of women with chronic hypertension took aspirin as recommended by the national guidelines. This scenario is unlikely to improve unless policy-makers incorporate a feasible universal PE screening program with effective prophylactic measures based on individualized screening results, in line with recent recommendations from the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics (FIGO),(11) the International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (ISSHP),(12) and the International Society of Ultrasound in Obstetrics and Gynecology (ISUOG).(13) Although the best predictive performance using the FMF algorithm is achieved with Doppler ultrasound, settings without this tool can pragmatically calculate the risk of PE using maternal characteristics, clinical history, and mean arterial pressure, as recommended by FIGO.(11) The Concept Foundation is conducting a large trial in three African countries and India to validate a simplified version of the FMF algorithm (maternal factors plus mean arterial pressure) to make its use possible even in low- and middle-income countries.(14) In Brazil, the FMF algorithm with biophysical and without biochemical markers was previously validated and achieved a detection rate of 71%,(15) similar to the reference study.(16)

Regarding calcium supplementation during pregnancy, the latest Cochrane meta-analysis shows that current evidence does not support its use in PE prophylaxis.(17) Previous suggestions that calcium is effective in preventing PE originate from small randomized trials that are prone to bias and likely to overestimate treatment effects, and have not been confirmed in larger trials that represent 88% of the data on calcium to prevent PE.(18)

Despite concerns about translating findings from experimental studies into real-world practice, the results of the present study cannot be generalized or allowed to undermine the implementation in Brazil of the only effective and reproducible intervention capable of mitigating preeclampsia and its consequences, namely, effective early screening and low-dose aspirin prophylaxis for high-risk individuals, including those with chronic hypertension and a high-risk screening result.

body.p: We thank the authors of the letter to the editors for their thoughtful comments on our recently published article "Low adherence to aspirin and calcium carbonate for preeclampsia prevention in pregnant women with chronic hypertension in a Brazilian hospital".(1) We welcome the opportunity to clarify the objectives of our study and address the points raised.

The primary goal of our study was to evaluate adherence to preeclampsia prophylaxis among pregnant women with chronic hypertension. In this context, the low adherence observed is, in itself, a highly relevant finding, particularly in a setting where hypertensive disorder of pregnancy is the leading causes of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality.(2) Among the barriers to the use of prophylactic measures, limited awareness among pregnant women regarding the indication and importance of these interventions is a well-recognized factor, especially in low- and middle-income countries, reinforcing the need for health education strategies and for stronger communication between healthcare professionals and patients.(3)

We were, however, surprised by the high incidence of preeclampsia even among women with good adherence to aspirin. Chronic hypertension is a well-established high-risk factor for the development of preeclampsia and, on its own, is a strong indication for prophylaxis.(4) Therefore, we agree that the recommendation for low-dose aspirin remains supported by national and international guidelines and should continue to be followed in clinical practice.(5-7)

From a pathophysiological perspective, preeclampsia superimposed on chronic hypertension represents a distinct clinical phenotype, frequently associated with pre-existing vascular disease, obesity, metabolic and endothelial dysfunction.(8,9) In this context, mechanisms targeted by aspirin in early placentation may play a less central role, which could partially explain the more limited and inconsistent preventive effect observed in women with chronic hypertension as reported in previous studies.(10,11) Moreover, chronic hypertension in pregnancy often coexists with other metabolic conditions such as obesity (> 30 kg/m² BMI), which has been shown to reduce the effectiveness of aspirin in pregnant women.(12) Importantly, this does not invalidate the recommendation for aspirin across guidelines; rather, it suggests that, in addition to aspirin and calcium when indicated, complementary strategies to optimize blood pressure control and address modifiable risk factors should be encouraged.(13,14)

The authors refer to a recent secondary analysis of the ASPRE trial suggesting that, in women with chronic hypertension, aspirin may shift the distribution of gestational age at delivery with preeclampsia to later gestational ages.(15) Although a shift in gestational age was observed, a significant reduction in the incidence of preterm preeclampsia was not demonstrated in this population.(15) We acknowledge the clinical of potentially delaying the earliest cases of preeclampsia. However, it is important to emphasize that the ASPRE trial was not designed or powered to specifically evaluate women with chronic hypertension, and the authors themselves acknowledge the limited statistical power for this subgroup.(11)

Regarding calcium supplementation, we agree that the evidence supporting its use for preeclampsia prevention in this subgroup is limited, which restricts conclusions about the magnitude of its potential benefit. It is also worth noting that, at the time our manuscript was written and submitted, the most recent Cochrane review on calcium supplementation had not yet been published.(16) These findings reinforce the need to continuously re-evaluate recommended interventions as new evidence emerges and to ensure that preventive strategies are both effective and evidence based.

The authors also mention screening using the Fetal Medicina Foundation (FMF) algorithm with Doppler and biochemical markers. Although the combined FMF screening model demonstrates excellent performance, it is important to consider the balance between incremental predictive gain and feasibility in real-world settings. Recent systematic evaluations show that the FMF model achieves a summary AUC of 0.90 (95% PI, 0.76–0.97) when combining maternal factors with biochemical markers and uterine artery Doppler, whereas models based on maternal factors alone have an AUC of 0.77 (95% PI, 0.68–0.84), increasing to 0.84 (95% PI, 0.82–0.85) with the addition of mean arterial pressure.(17) In this context, the added value of universal Doppler assessment and biochemical testing may be modest when weighed against cost, infrastructure requirements, and logistical complexity, particularly in low-middle-income countries. Furthermore, in women with chronic hypertension, the condition itself already indicates aspirin prophylaxis; therefore, it may be more impactful to prioritize strategies that improve awareness and adherence. In our study, a substantial proportion of participants were unaware of maternal (34.7%), and fetal (23.5%) complications related to preeclampsia, underscoring the need to strengthen counseling and health education efforts.

Finally, we reiterate that our study primarily aimed to describe low adherence to prophylactic measures for preeclampsia; the observed preeclampsia incidence was a secondary finding that drew our attention. We believe these data may contribute to the ongoing debate on prophylaxis, inform strategies to increase adherence, and support the implementation of complementary preventive measures, ultimately improving maternal and perinatal outcomes.

The low adherence observed in our study highlights the need to strengthen educational strategies and patient counseling regarding the rationale, potential benefits, and safety of aspirin use during pregnancy. Improving awareness and patient engagement is a key step toward maximizing the impact of existing preventive measures.

We would like to emphasize that our findings should not be interpreted as a reason to discourage the use of low-dose aspirin in women with chronic hypertension. Given the high baseline risk of preeclampsia in this population and current guideline recommendations,(5-7) aspirin prophylaxis should continue to be encouraged and remains a cornerstone of prevention in high-risk pregnancies.
